analysis.one_liner: Lets foreign-flag ships carry cargo between the mainland and Alaska, Hawaii, and U.S. territories.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee in April 2023 and died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: A century-old law called the Jones Act says cargo moving between U.S. ports must travel on ships that were built in the United States, are mostly owned by U.S. citizens, and are mostly crewed by them. Because only a small fleet of such ships exists, shipping costs to places like Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and Guam run far above international rates, and those costs show up in food, fuel, and store prices. This bill would open those specific routes to foreign-flag ships, as long as the operators follow U.S. labor and environmental rules, pay U.S. taxes, accept lawsuits in U.S. courts, and provide injury coverage for their crews. It never advanced past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other territories, who pay a shipping premium on nearly everything they import, would benefit from competition that could bring rates closer to international levels. Foreign-flag shipping lines would gain access to a market previously closed to them.

how_it_helps.text: Allows qualifying foreign-flag freight vessels to carry merchandise between a mainland port and a port in Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, or a U.S. territory, and between two noncontiguous ports — routes currently reserved by law for U.S.-built, U.S.-owned, U.S.-crewed ships.

Conditions the exception on real obligations: foreign operators must employ U.S. citizens as required of registered vessels, meet minimum international labor standards for seafarers, comply with the same environmental standards as U.S. vessels, name an agent for service of process, abide by U.S. tax laws, keep documentation aboard, and face injury and death lawsuits in U.S. district court near where the injury occurred.
Lets foreign operators enroll their masters and crew members in the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation program, so injured seafarers would have a defined compensation route.

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flag shipping companies and U.S. shipyards, which today hold a legal monopoly on domestic waterborne cargo and charge rates well above the international market. Their crews — and the unions representing them — would face competition from lower-wage foreign crews, and shipyards would lose guaranteed demand for U.S.-built Jones Act vessels. Supporters of the current law also argue the U.S.-flag fleet and shipyard base are national-security assets that a smaller fleet would erode.
analysis.who_pays_short: U.S.-flag shippers, shipyards, and maritime crews

drawbacks.text: Foreign crews are generally paid far less than U.S. crews; opening the routes could move maritime jobs from U.S. workers to foreign crews, even though the bill imposes international labor minimums and a compensation program on the foreign operators.

The U.S.-flag fleet and the shipyards that build for it are treated as strategic assets for military sealift in a crisis; shrinking their guaranteed domestic market could weaken that capacity — the core argument for the Jones Act.
Enforcement of the bill's labor, environmental, and tax conditions depends on regulating companies based abroad, which in practice is harder than regulating U.S. operators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories, the benefit would be direct and ongoing: competition on routes where a small protected fleet currently sets prices. The costs — pressure on U.S. maritime jobs, shipyard demand, and the sealift fleet — are real and fall on a specific, politically protected industry, which is exactly why versions of this exemption have been proposed for years and never passed. The bill tries to blunt the objection by attaching labor, environmental, tax, and court-jurisdiction requirements to foreign operators.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then a maritime subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case, a Democrat from Hawaii, introduced the bill on April 13, 2023, together with Rep. James Moylan, the Republican delegate from Guam.
It was referred the same day to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and, for the labor provisions, to the Education and the Workforce Committee.
Four days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, which was its last action of record.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote was ever scheduled, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still in committee.
Moylan was the bill's only cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S.-flag shipping companies and U.S. shipyards that hold the Jones Act monopoly are better off, since their protected domestic market stays closed to foreign competition. Island consumers keep paying the higher shipping rates embedded in their cost of living.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: U.S.-flag shipping companies and U.S. shipyards

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.role: U.S. Representative for Hawaii, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt noncontiguous shipping routes from the Jones Act's U.S.-built, U.S.-owned, U.S.-crewed requirements.

for.name: Rep. James Moylan
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor, representing a territory that pays the Jones Act shipping premium.

against.name: Rep. Sam Graves
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee received the referral in April 2023 and never reported the bill, held a hearing, or scheduled a markup.

against.name: U.S.-flag shipping companies and maritime labor unions
against.role: Jones Act carriers, shipyards, and seafarer unions defending the domestic shipping protection
against.what_they_did: Have long lobbied Congress to preserve the Jones Act's shipbuilding, ownership, and crewing requirements, which underpin their domestic market.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Hawaii Democrat and the only cosponsor a Guam Republican, but with two sponsors total and no recorded votes, the fight never grew large enough to show a partisan split.

industries.note: These carriers hold a legal monopoly on cargo between U.S. ports and charge rates well above international levels, a premium paid in the price of goods in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories. The bill would let foreign-flag vessels compete on those routes.
The Jones Act requires domestic cargo ships to be U.S.-built, guaranteeing shipyards a captive market for a small, expensive fleet. Foreign competition would cut into that guaranteed demand.

industries.industry: Maritime labor (U.S. seafarers and their unions)
industries.note: U.S. crew jobs on noncontiguous routes would face competition from foreign crews paid under international standards, though the bill requires minimum labor standards and compensation coverage for those crews.
They would gain entry to a large domestic market previously closed to them, and their interest in winning that cargo runs alongside consumers' interest in cheaper shipping.

industries.industry: Import-dependent retailers and businesses in noncontiguous areas
industries.note: Lower freight rates would reduce their landed costs and, in turn, prices for island residents.
